events.text:
🇺🇦 ⚠️ 🇺🇸 #Musk Asked #Trump To Slow Down #Ukraine's Military Defenses, Telegraph Exclusive Reveals: 
Elon Musk approached Donald Trump with the idea of slowing down Starlink in Ukraine, The Telegraph can reveal.
The billionaire tech entrepreneur approached the US president with the proposal to introduce speed limits on the system, which hampered Ukraine’s drone defences, according to four sources familiar with the discussions
One of the sources said Mr Trump “agreed” with Mr Musk’s suggestion, paving the way for the Pentagon to execute the slowdown on Starshield.
Mr Musk had previously blamed Mr Trump for the chaos, claiming any changes would have been decided by the US military and ultimately the president.
At the time, Mr Trump was embroiled in a row with Volodymyr Zelensky over Ukraine’s strikes on Russian oil refineries.
US officials had warned Kyiv’s team of peace negotiators that the U.S. could shut off intelligence-sharing and other kinds of support if the long-range attacks were not halted. 
Earlier this week, one of Mr Zelensky’s advisers said Mr Musk’s SpaceX had restricted access to the Starshield system, used by Kyiv to intercept jet-powered drones and strike behind enemy lines.
Speaking on the fringes of an EU summit on Friday, the Ukrainian president called the slowdown a “very dangerous and unpleasant surprise”.
Mr Musk denied he was responsible for limiting Starlink access, blaming the White House. He claimed that “any limits on speed or usage” were “decided by the US military and ultimately POTUS”, referring to Mr Trump.
However, after what was described as a “night of carnage” in Kyiv because of the blackout, a senior source said Mr Musk had been alarmed about the possibility of adverse consumer reaction in Europe.
The source said: “He tweeted out that he was innocent and that it was the US administration that did it. The reality is that they were both in it.”
A high-ranking European official and two well-placed Ukrainian sources confirmed this version of events.
Speaking on Friday evening, Mr Trump said he did not think ‌either ‌he ⁠nor Mr Musk had been responsible for Ukraine ⁠losing Starlink access.
On Friday, an anonymous US official, cited in a report by the AFP, insisted that Trump did not make the request for a reduction of Starshield’s services for Ukraine. “No request was ever made by the president,” the US official said, after a report by Reuters claimed the decision came from the White House. 
The Pentagon has not publicly explained the restrictions.
The speed cap imposed on Ukraine limited drones using the Starshield system to around 160kmph, making it virtually impossible to intercept Russia’s barrages of jet-powered drones and missiles, which travel double the speed.
On Friday, Mr Zelensky said signals were being restored.
It is not the first time Mr Musk has been accused of limiting the use of his Starlink platform to the detriment of Ukraine.
In 2023, he confirmed he had rebutted requests by Kyiv to use the system in drone attacks on Crimea, the peninsula illegally annexed by Russia, to avoid being complicit in a “major act of war”.
Mr Musk was lauded by Ukrainians earlier this year for his direct role in blocking illegal access to Starlink by Russian soldiers fighting in Ukraine.
Radek Sikorski, Poland’s foreign minister, warned the tech billionaire: “As your European customers, we are watching you.”
The EU is planning to have its Iris2, a Starlink replacement, operational by 2030. Mr Zelensky arrived in Brussels bruised and seeking more support from his European allies after his war of words with Mr Trump.
Diplomats said leaders had advised the Ukrainian president to tone down his criticism of his US counterpart amid fears Washington could further withdraw its support for Kyiv.
Mr Trump has been highly critical of Ukraine’s strikes on Russia’s oil refineries, blaming them for soaring energy prices before the midterm elections next month.
More: www.telegraph.co.uk/world-news/2026/10/16/musk-approached-trump-slow-down-starlink-help-ukraine/

Weapons used:
SM-6 missiles from the destroyer USS Paul Ignatius (DDG-117)
Naval Strike Missile (NSM) missiles from the frigate Portland (F79)
Sea Venom missiles (Royal Navy)
Mk 48 torpedoes from the submarine Massachusetts (SSN-798)
The exercise also involved P-8 aircraft of the U.S. Navy and the Royal Air Force, as well as F-15E fighters of the U.S. Air Force.
The frigate Klakring belonged to the Oliver Hazard Perry class and served in the U.S. Navy from 1983 to 2013. It was named after Rear Admiral Thomas Klakring, a three‑time recipient of the Navy Cross who commanded the submarine Guardfish during World War II.
These drills were also the first time the Royal Navy used its new NSM and Sea Venom anti‑ship missiles against a real target.

🇾🇪🇸🇦 'Davos in the desert' called off as Houthi attacks hit Saudi airports
Saudi Arabia has called off its flagship Future Investment Initiative, the annual gathering known as "Davos in the desert," following a wave of Houthi attacks on Saudi airports, Financial Times reports.
The event, which was due to start next week, will now take place next year. Organizers had reportedly considered holding the event virtually on the original dates but decided to postpone it entirely.
👉 The FII is one of the Gulf's most high-profile gatherings. Over the past decade, it has become Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman's premier platform for pitching his Vision 2030 economic diversification agenda to the world's most powerful financiers and executives. The postponement is a significant setback for the country's efforts to project calm and attract foreign capital at a time when [its economy is already under strain](https://t.me/geopolitics_prime/76203) from the conflict. 
The Houthis have continued to inflict [painful blows](https://t.me/geopolitics_prime/76454) on Saudi-backed forces despite months of airstrikes and a large-scale counteroffensive. On October 19, three Houthi ballistic missiles struck a military training camp in Shabwa province, killing at least 53 soldiers and wounding more than 200, according to local authorities.
👉 This is not the first time the FII has been disrupted. In 2021, most international attendees participated virtually because of COVID-related travel restrictions, with the event adopting a hybrid format. Three years earlier, in 2018, a string of high-profile executives pulled out of the summit following the killing of journalist Jamal Khashoggi by Saudi agents.

⚔️ Why can’t Saudi Arabia beat the Houthis? Its military is stuck planning for a 20th century war
 
Despite ranking as the world’s third-largest defense spender for much of the past decade, and fielding the most sophisticated US hardware available anywhere outside Israel and NATO, Saudi Arabia has proven helpless against a besandaled Yemeni resistance group armed mostly with light arms, simple ballistic missiles and drones.
 
The disconnect comes down to three factors, says Princeton Middle East researcher Bernard Haykel:
1️⃣ the fact that Saudi Arabia has been planning for a traditional, 1990-1991 Gulf War-style war, not a regional asymmetric conflict.
2️⃣ “deliberate weakening” of the Saudi military in the 50s and 60s to “coup-proof the regime.”
3️⃣ rabid factionalism – with different princes controlling different elements of the military.
“It wasn’t a kind of force that was coordinated, and didn’t have a culture of meritocracy…MBS has been trying to change this in the last decade, but it’s a culture that’s very deeply ingrained and very difficult to change,” Haykel explained.
 
He didn’t mention it, but there are also other factors accounting for Ansar Allah’s staying power:
 
🔴 Saudi Arabia’s reliance on overpriced, overly complex and underperforming [US weapons systems](https://t.me/geopolitics_prime/76242).
🔴 Riyadh’s dependence on air power, contractors and [regional proxies](https://t.me/geopolitics_prime/74783), compared to a battle-hardened Yemeni guerrilla force that’s survived Saudi, UAE, US, UK and Israeli bombardment and a crushing blockade for over a decade.
🔴 the much wealthier Saudi rentier society’s aversion to hardship, casualties, and [sacrifice](https://t.me/geopolitics_prime/76203) compared to the Yemenis.
🔴 Ansar Allah’s [network of mountain fortresses](https://t.me/geopolitics_prime/76197), which make their defeat from the air impossible, and a ground campaign much too costly.

👁 I see you: Russian satellite hot on the trail of NATO orbital spy feeding info to Ukraine
 
OSINT trackers have spotted Russia’s Cosmos 2612 satellite approaching to within a few km of ICEYE-X36 (NORAD ID 59103) – a Finnish SAR satellite providing Earth observation data to the US government and military, other militaries, and defense contractors.
♦️ Swiss real-time space domain awareness tracker s2a systems calculates that the Russian spacecraft was just ~5km from ICEYE’s craft as they flew over South America on Sunday, perfectly matching its trajectory at speeds of ~27.3k km/h, 550 km above the planet.
♦️With the Russian craft matching ICEYE’s geometric plane, it may prove difficult, if not impossible, for the Finnish satellite to escape.
Russia hasn't disclosed much about Cosmos 2612 since launching it from Plesetsk in April, but Western observers suspect it's designed to approach other satellites, inspect them and gather intelligence.
❗️Getting this close opens up some interesting possibilities. 
➡️ Positioned at close range, the satellite could glean vital electronic and operational data, intercept and analyze radio frequencies, signal patterns and telemetry, map communications architecture to ease jamming, and deduce exactly when and how often Ukraine requests real-time imagery.
➡️ If it’s equipped with a close-range EW package, it could even engage in signal spoofing, inject malicious telemetry data to turn ICEYE’s cameras away from Ukraine, fall into safe mode, burn fuel needlessly, or disrupt signal flows.
Reports on the Russian satellite’s stalking of the ICEYE spacecraft comes in the wake of[ Starlink’s](https://t.me/geopolitics_prime/76194) decision to introduce speed caps on the Ukrainian military’s systems, which have seriously hampered its offensive capabilities.

🇷🇺🪖Ukraine’s air defenses fail to intercept a single Russian ballistic missile in overnight strikes
 
Russian Iskander-M missiles and S-400s repurposed for ground attack missions slipped through Ukraine’s defenses unmolested, with hits reported across 25 locations, and “debris” recorded at eight more, the Ukrainian Air Force’s official Telegram channel admitted.
The missiles were reportedly launched in combination with Iskander-K cruise missiles and 269 Geran-type strike UAVs (59 of them jet powered) as well as Banderol, Gerbera and other drones. The Air Force claims to have brought down 247 of the non-ballistic targets using aviation, AA troops, EW, unmanned systems and mobile fire groups.
But reporting, photos and videos from the ground tell a different story, with Russia [hammering Ukraine’s energy grid](https://t.me/geopolitics_prime/76341),[ industrial infrastructure](https://t.me/geopolitics_prime/76132), [ports, bridges, logistics, and military infrastructure](https://t.me/geopolitics_prime/75930) for months on end, leaving entire sectors of the economy on the brink of collapse, and [the war effort increasingly crippled](https://t.me/geopolitics_prime/76238).
On Monday, Ukrainian telecoms giant Datagroup announced a devastating Russian night strike on its main data center, saying “repairing it and resuming operations are impossible.”
Ukraine’s troubles have been compounded by its Patriot missile interceptors[ running dry](https://t.me/geopolitics_prime/76246), and by Elon Musk’s decision to slap speed restrictions on its Starlink connection – whose strategic impact has been compared to[ a ‘nuclear strike’](https://t.me/geopolitics_prime/76224) by local commanders.

💣 Houthi attacks expose cracks in Saudi Arabia’s multi-billion-dollar defenses - report
Despite having one of the world's largest defense budgets and a hangar full of top-notch US fighters and air-defense systems, Saudi Arabia is still failing to stop Houthi missiles and drones from hammering its capital and oil facilities, The Wall Street Journal reports.
Here’s what’s being exposed by the Houthi strikes:
➡️ A shortage of interceptors is crippling Saudi air defenses
➡️ The US is providing intelligence only — no direct military help
➡️ Trump suggested taking Israeli assistance, but Saudi Arabia stayed silent
➡️ Now the kingdom is scrambling for support from Turkey, Pakistan, European countries and Egypt
The Houthis keep churning out their own missiles and drones, and hide production deep underground, while constantly repositioning their launchers. They readily absorb Saudi airstrikes and hit various soft targets deep inside the kingdom.
Saudi Arabia's sheer geographic size is its Achilles' heel. Oil facilities, civilian airports and other critical infrastructure lie scattered across vast desert expanses, offering Houthi missiles and drones a target-rich landscape of unguarded gaps.
As former US ambassador to Saudi Arabia Michael Ratney put it, Riyadh will eventually need an off-ramp. The Houthis have already proven they can inflict serious damage through asymmetric warfare.

🇦🇺 Australia to arm underwater drones with sea mines and aerial UAVs
Australia is developing new payloads for its autonomous naval drones, including sea mines and uncrewed aerial vehicles, Defense Minister Richard Marles and Defense Industry Minister Pat Conroy announced.
Ghost Shark underwater drones will be able to carry a range of mission-specific payloads, including supply caches, sea mines and aerial drones.
👉 The upgrades will also extend to Speartooth and BlueBottle unmanned surface vessels.
The systems are designed for underwater combat, seabed operations, restricting enemy access to maritime areas and protecting critical undersea infrastructure.
Under its 2026 defense strategy, Australia plans to invest up to $4 billion over 10 years in autonomous and unmanned underwater warfare capabilities, including around $1.2 billion for a fleet of Ghost Shark vehicles.

🇺🇸 Big threats, thin stockpiles: Pentagon’s most powerful bombs running out
As Donald Trump reportedly weighs the use of the [GBU-43/B MOAB bomb](https://t.me/geopolitics_prime/76228), the 21,000-pound weapon nicknamed the "mother of all bombs," in a potential new round of strikes on Iranian energy infrastructure and nuclear facilities, the stockpile of the Pentagon's most powerful penetrating weapons is alarmingly thin.
The US may have only a low-single-digit number of GBU-57 Massive Ordnance Penetrators left, an analysis from the Center for Strategic and International Studies estimates. The 30,000-pound bomb, designed to destroy deeply buried targets, was used 14 times against Iranian nuclear facilities during Operation Midnight Hammer in June 2025. The Pentagon has redirected $123 million toward replenishing the inventory, but new bombs will take years to arrive.
The "mother of all bombs" is even scarcer. The US built about a dozen of the GBU-43/B, one of which was used in 2017 against an Islamic State cave complex in Afghanistan. Around 10 should remain. But despite its size, the MOAB cannot penetrate as deeply as the GBU-57.
Meanwhile, Iran entrenches its high-value military facilities by burrowing further underground to put them beyond the reach of conventional weapons. Previous US attacks showed that even when targets were hit, the bombs inflicted very[ limited damage](https://t.me/geopolitics_prime/68755) and the facilities kept operating.
🔴 CSIS highlights reports of 33 underground Iranian missile bases near the Strait of Hormuz, many of which have survived earlier American attacks or are being rapidly [rebuilt at the moment ](https://t.me/geopolitics_prime/70379)
🔴 Iran's Pickaxe Mountain nuclear complex near Natanz may be buried so deeply inside a granite mountain that even the GBU-57 could struggle to reach it
The US retains a large inventory of smaller 2,000-pound bunker busters, but inventory stress is greatest with the largest munitions. Current bunker busters are nearly all free-fall bombs, which require delivery aircraft to fly over the target — exposing the carrier aircraft to attack.
